reason: Document A lays out each step by trigger, action, data kept and failure response, and adds a full failure table and a limits table, so a newcomer sees the whole system without wading through definitions of cookies, status codes and transactions that a technical reader already knows, though B's table schemas and sliding-window example are real strengths.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to learn from: it starts with how the system works today and what stack it runs on, then takes each flow in turn (what triggers it, what it does, what data it keeps, how it fails), and adds a failures table and a limits table for quick lookup; A spends a lot of space defining basics a smart engineer already knows and packs the actual behavior into a dense decisions table.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts by stating the current system: a server-rendered app, two instances with no sticky sessions, and an existing users table. It then defines its terms, gives the full schema, and walks through each step with what triggers it, what it stores and how it fails. B depends on a numbered requirements list that a newcomer never sees, and it lists its tables in shorthand.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow for a newcomer: its steps run strictly in order, with no exceptions to remember (A says to run 16 and 17 before 12, and 15 before 14), and its "key A/key B" and "v1/v2 image" names make the mixed-fleet and rollback states concrete. reason: B gives a newcomer a better start: it describes the current state concretely, defines terms like pod, readiness probe and canary, names the new component, numbers every step in one sequence with cross-references, and ends with a failure table, although A's runtime-first order is tighter.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains why keys can't change today (they are read once at import into a singleton), defines the basic terms a newcomer would need (pod, readiness probe, canary), numbers its steps 1-15 across both parts so cross-references are unambiguous, and ends with a failure summary table, so it is easier to build a mental model from than B, which is tighter but restarts its numbering in each part and assumes more background.

author: haiku
reason: Document A's numbered steps match its detailed diagrams one to one, it covers the email worker's own flow, and its failure table is consistent; Document B introduces the parts more gently, but its step numbering contradicts itself ("steps 2 to 7", "4 to 9" and "6 to 8" all name the transaction) and its flow diagrams are vaguer.

author: haiku
reason: Document A suits a newcomer better: it opens with what the feature does, lists each part of the system and its role, defines even basic terms such as transaction and row lock, and walks through short, separate diagrams. author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to pick up cold: it opens with a plain summary of the feature, describes the existing system, defines its terms, and lists what is still undecided before showing the flows, while A puts you straight into a dense ASCII block with no introduction.

reason: B is written for someone new to the project: it defines the stack terms (OIDC, PKCE, state and nonce, GETDEL, TTL, unique violation) and walks through the diagram in prose, and it explains why things work as they do (the invariant, SameSite=Lax, how races are resolved), while A is precise and well structured but assumes the reader already knows OIDC and Redis.

author: haiku
reason: A suits a newcomer better: it opens with a plain-language overview and defines every unfamiliar mechanism it uses (PKCE, state, nonce, GETDEL, TTL, the lockout rule), then explains the diagram's tricky parts, such as the race handling, the invariant and why the cookie is SameSite=Lax. B assumes more OIDC background and contradicts itself: step 2 says a bad state is the only case that gets an error page, yet code-exchange and token failures also get one.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow on its own: it defines basic terms such as replica, snapshot, MERGE and transaction, has one diagram that covers every store and job (staleness check, dashboards, reconciliation), and explains why it makes key choices, such as using the snapshot clock as the high-water mark and the lookback argument; A is crisper about failure handling but assumes more prior context.

reason: B is easier to build a mental model from: each step says what starts it, what it does, where its data lives and what happens on failure, and it adds a table of who writes each piece of state, a failure table, the actual MERGE SQL and a clear window rule for retries, while A puts the whole system into one dense diagram and long bullet lists.

author: sonnet
reason: A gives the cleaner first mental model, but B answers more of the questions a newcomer would ask next: it explains the lock mechanism (a partial unique index), the timeouts, how a stale or late attempt is handled and what happens if the runner dies, and each step lists what starts it, what it does, which data it touches and what happens on failure; it also says what recon cannot fix and lists open questions.

author: haiku
reason: Document A starts with a flow diagram and a one-line role for each component, and it explains stack terms a newcomer won't know (consumer group, acks = all, idempotent producer, TTL, watermark), so the mental model forms quickly; Document B's consistent Starts/Does/Keeps/If-goes-wrong steps are thorough, but it has no picture and adds more concepts (seal, cutoff, day states, winners, late events) before you can see the whole system.

author: sonnet

author: sonnet
reason: A gives a newcomer the mental model faster: its diagram separates the live and replay paths cleanly, and its "Decisions that shape everything" section explains why each core choice was made (day by received_at, hashing on event_id, the archive as source of truth) before the steps begin, whereas B covers failures more thoroughly but is harder to absorb because of its tangled single diagram and its repetitive Starts/Does/Data/If-it-goes-wrong template.
